entries.clue: Feline, wild being on the moor, only tail glimpsed (7)

indicatorNotes.only tail glimpsed: A tail is the end of a thing, and if only that much is seen you are left with the final letter and nothing else.

blocks.note: Pan, the goat-legged Greek god of woods and flocks, is the wild one
used as it stands
the last letter of mooR

annotation.surface: A big cat out on the moor, seen for only as long as its tail took to vanish.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wild' reads as a description of the beast and names a god instead. Bodmin Moor is where Cornwall's big-cat sightings keep being reported, which is why the surface sounds like a local newspaper.
annotation.definitionFit: The black leopard is a cat, so 'feline' names the answer only by its family and leaves the moorland beast of the surface to hint which one.

entries.clue: Coming from Europe – like staff? (6)

blocks.note: Poland is a European country and this is the adjective for anything out of it
a staff is a pole, and an -ish ending on a word means 'somewhat like it'

annotation.surface: Wondering whether the new arrival from the continent is one of the employees.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Staff' is the walking-stick sense, not the personnel of the surface. The second half only works if you read the answer as a pole with -ish tacked on, the E lost in the join — the liberty the question mark is there to buy.
annotation.definitionFit: Poland is in Europe, so its adjective covers the first half; split differently the word reads 'somewhat pole-like', and a staff is a pole.

entries.clue: Around Land’s End, lack of Spanish enthusiasm it seems for pasta (6)

indicatorNotes.Around: To be around a thing is to sit on both sides of it, so the letters given next close over the piece they are put around.

blocks.clueFragment: lack of Spanish enthusiasm it seems
blocks.note: olé is the Spanish shout of approval, so no olé is enthusiasm withheld; the five letters open after three
the end of the word LanD, while Land's End itself is the granite tip of Cornwall

annotation.surface: Nobody down at the far tip of Cornwall can raise much excitement about a plate of pasta.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Land's End' does two jobs at once, the Cornish headland of the surface and the last letter of the word 'Land'. Accents are ignored in crossword letters, so olé hands over a plain OLE.
annotation.definitionFit: A noodle is a ribbon or string of pasta, so 'pasta' is the material it is made of standing in for the thing itself.

entries.clue: Performance of the ode encapsulates style of fast-paced walk (4-3-3)

indicatorNotes.Performance: A performance of a piece is one particular rendering of it, and a rendering is free to set the parts out in a different order.
indicatorNotes.encapsulates: To encapsulate something is to shut it up inside a capsule, so the letters close right round the piece named next.

blocks.note: the six letters of 'the ode' in a new order, opened after the first two
élan is style, dash, the flair a thing is done with

annotation.surface: A staging of an ode said to contain a certain stylishness.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Style' looks like the start of the definition — a style of walk — and it is a piece of the wordplay instead, the French word for flair. The answer is the racewalker's rule, not a brisk stroll.
annotation.definitionFit: Heel-and-toe is the racewalking gait in which the front heel lands before the back toe lifts, the technique that keeps walking races fast yet legal.

entries.clue: Very uplifting southern puzzle (5)

indicatorNotes.uplifting: In a down entry, to be lifted up is to be read the other way, from the bottom of the answer towards the top.

blocks.note: über is German for very and English has borrowed it for uber-cool and the rest; here it climbs the grid backwards
s is the compass abbreviation for southern

annotation.surface: Something very inspiring down in the south.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition does no cryptic work at all, so the whole clue rests on spotting the borrowed German behind 'very'. 'Uplifting' passes for praise while telling you to read upwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A rebus is the puzzle that spells a phrase out in pictures and letters — a drawn eye and a tin can reading as 'I can'.

entries.clue: Serene icon punched by a cleaner (7)

indicatorNotes.punched by: To be punched by something is to have a hole driven into you, and whatever drove it ends up inside.

blocks.note: a pic is a picture, and an icon on a screen is a small one; the three letters split after the first
A followed by Cif, the cream cleanser on British kitchen sinks, sold as Jif until 2001

annotation.surface: A revered image taking a thump from the person doing the housework.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cleaner' is the trap: it reads as the one with the mop and it is a bottle of scouring cream. The definition wants the ordinary adjective, not the ocean the same word names.
annotation.definitionFit: Pacific is the adjective for peaceable and untroubled — a pacific temperament is a serene one — and the ocean was named for exactly that quality.

entries.clue: Remarkably sharp jackets I detect for ancient sect (9)

indicatorNotes.Remarkably: Something remarkable has departed from the usual, and letters that depart from their usual places spell something else.
indicatorNotes.jackets: To jacket a thing is to put a coat round it, so the letters before this word close over what comes after.

blocks.note: the five letters of 'sharp' in a new order, opened after four to take something in
I, then SEE for detect, the four letters that go inside

annotation.surface: A remarkably keen eye for tailoring: sharp jackets spotted at a glance.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Jackets' is the sort of noun that slides into a verb unnoticed — clothing in the surface, an instruction to wrap in the cryptic reading. 'I' is a letter here, not the speaker doing the detecting.
annotation.definitionFit: The Pharisees were the strict, law-keeping Jewish party the Gospels set against Jesus, so 'ancient sect' names them by their age and kind.

entries.clue: Murderer in good book residing in Jamaica Inn (4)

indicatorNotes.residing in: Something residing in a place is living inside it, and here the letters are living inside the two words that follow.

blocks.note: JamaiCA INn — the run of letters crosses the gap between the two words

annotation.surface: A killer holed up at Jamaica Inn.
annotation.walkthrough: Jamaica Inn is the real coaching house on Bodmin Moor that gave Daphne du Maurier her smugglers' novel, so a murderer sounds at home there and the letters go unnoticed. 'Good book' is the Bible.
annotation.definitionFit: Cain killed his brother Abel in Genesis, which makes him the first murderer in the Bible — the good book of the definition.

entries.clue: Nut and oaf dancing in spring (8)

indicatorNotes.dancing: Dancers keep changing places, so letters told to dance will not be standing where they started.

blocks.note: the six letters of 'nut' and 'oaf' in a new order, with 'and' doing nothing but joining them
used as it stands

annotation.surface: A fool and a dolt having a dance in springtime.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like the word that puts the dancing somewhere and it is two letters of the answer, tacked on the end. 'Spring' is water, not the season the surface offers.
annotation.definitionFit: Fountain keeps its older sense of a source of water — the fountainhead of a river is where it rises — so a spring is the same thing.

entries.clue: Put together with jam ultimately covered, a Cornish treat (5,3)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: What comes ultimately comes last, so the word beside it gives up its final letter only.
indicatorNotes.covered: Something covered has another thing laid over it, so this letter vanishes inside the piece it is put into.

blocks.note: to create is to put a thing together; these six letters open after four
the last letter of jaM
used as it stands, and it belongs to the wordplay rather than to the definition

annotation.surface: Assembling a Cornish treat with the jam ending up buried.
annotation.walkthrough: The 'a' reads as the start of 'a Cornish treat' and is a letter of the answer instead, which is why the definition is two words rather than three. In Cornwall the jam goes on the scone before the cream; in Devon it goes on after, and people mind.
annotation.definitionFit: A cream tea is scones served with clotted cream and jam, and Cornwall is the county that claims it, so 'Cornish treat' names it by where it belongs.

entries.clue: Debauched son in Cornish town (5)

indicatorNotes.in: The plain word does the work: what comes before it goes in among the letters named after it.

blocks.note: Looe is the twin-harbour fishing town on the south Cornish coast; its four letters split after three
s is the family-tree abbreviation for son

annotation.surface: A wayward son sent off to a small town in Cornwall.
annotation.walkthrough: Cornish place names are the puzzle's running joke, and this one hides in plain sight because 'Cornish town' looks like the definition. The answer is the moral sense, as in loose living, not the untied one.
annotation.definitionFit: Loose in its moral use — loose living, a loose woman — is precisely 'debauched', a sense the word now keeps only in those phrases.

entries.clue: Joy sees what to do with 8 down, say, in Cornish town (9)

indicatorNotes.in: The plain word places one thing inside another: what has just been named goes within the letters that follow.

blocks.note: Bude is the surfing town on Cornwall's north coast, opened up after its first letter

blocks.clueFragment: what to do with 8 down, say
blocks.note: 8 down is a plateful, so the obvious thing to do with it is EAT IT

annotation.surface: The delight of knowing what to do with a Cornish treat once you are in Cornwall.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Say' marks eating it as merely one obvious thing to do with 8 down, which is the setter covering himself. Cross-references like this one are safest left until the other clue is filled.
annotation.definitionFit: A beatitude is a state of blessedness — the 'Blessed are...' verses of the Sermon on the Mount are the Beatitudes — and blessedness is joy of the settled kind.

entries.clue: Mischievous pals shut in leader’s office (10)

indicatorNotes.Mischievous: Mischief is making a mess of things for fun, and letters made mischief with will not stay in the order they were given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

annotation.surface: Playful friends locked inside the boss's room.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shut in' is bait — the best container indicator in the clue, and fodder instead — while the real instruction is the adjective standing in front of it. The answer names the post rather than the man, the way 'chairmanship' does.
annotation.definitionFit: A sultanship is the office and dominion held by a sultan, and a sultan is a leader, so the definition names the job rather than its holder.

entries.clue: Tiny amount, nothing to plug hole in the wall (4)

indicatorNotes.to plug: To plug a gap is to stop it up from inside, so the letter beside it drops into the middle of what follows.

blocks.note: hole in the wall is the British street name for a cash machine, whose initials open in the middle
the round letter stands for nothing, as on a scoreboard

annotation.surface: Having nothing at all left to feed into the cash machine in the wall.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface offers a wall with a hole in it and the clue wants the machine set into one. 'Tiny amount' is the figurative use, as in not an atom of truth.
annotation.definitionFit: An atom is the smallest particle going, and the idiom 'not an atom of' means not the least scrap of a thing, which is the sense the definition takes.

entries.clue: So, may hate going out, time taken inside? (4-2-4)

annotation.definition: So, may hate going out, time taken inside?

indicatorNotes.going out: Going out is leaving the place you were in, and letters that go out of their places come back in a different arrangement.
indicatorNotes.taken inside: Something taken inside is carried into the middle of a thing, so this letter joins the others from within.

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder
t is the standard abbreviation for time

annotation.surface: Someone who might dislike going out and would rather spend the time indoors.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word does two jobs here: read straight the sentence describes the very person the letters spell, and read as instructions it shuffles nine letters round a tenth. The question mark is the setter's flag for that double duty.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the whole clue is a description of a person who hates going out and spends their time indoors, which is exactly what the answer calls such a person.

entries.clue: Gone west, westernised drink! (7,4)

indicatorNotes.Gone west: To go west is to be lost or done for, and a word that has gone west no longer holds the order it came in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters, exactly the length the grid wants

annotation.surface: A drink that has gone west and been westernised on the way.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder wears its own indicator: 'gone west' and 'westernised' hold the same three-letter direction, and the exclamation mark is the setter admiring that. 'Drink' on its own is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A dessert wine is the sweet wine poured with the pudding — Sauternes, Tokaji — so 'drink' names it by the broadest category it belongs to.

entries.clue: Having bagged last of garbage, dumped metal stick with it (7,2)

indicatorNotes.Having bagged: To bag a thing is to get it into your bag, so whatever has bagged it keeps it inside.
indicatorNotes.last of: The last of a word is its final letter, and that is all this asks for.

blocks.note: to dump shares or a car is to sell them off in a hurry
iron is the everyday metal, and its four letters open after the first
the final letter of garbagE

annotation.surface: Someone who has pocketed the last of the rubbish and offloaded the scrap metal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stick with it' looks like more of the surface's clearing-up and is the definition instead, which is where the clue hides its join. 'Dumped' for sold is the stock-market sense — dumping a holding is offloading it fast.
annotation.definitionFit: To soldier on is to keep doggedly at something when stopping would be easier, which is what 'stick with it' urges — the infantryman's trudge behind both.

entries.clue: Robbers in briny leaving New York, Penzance pirates people? (8)

indicatorNotes.leaving: What leaves goes away, so the letters named next are taken out of the word in front of them.

blocks.note: the briny is the sea, five letters about to lose two
NY is the state abbreviation for New York, and those two letters come out
The Pirates of Penzance is Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera, so the people behind those pirates are G AND S

annotation.surface: Thieves out on the water, well away from New York, among the pirates of Penzance.
annotation.walkthrough: The last three words look like a definition and are a charade: two names and the word that always sits between them. Penzance is the Cornish port at the far end of the line from Paddington, which keeps the surface local.
annotation.definitionFit: Brigands are robbers who work in armed bands, the sort who held up travellers in wild country, so 'robbers' is the everyday word for them.

entries.clue: Criticise one tipster dressed for Royal Ascot? (3,3,2)

indicatorNotes.dressed: Somebody dressed has clothing round them, so the garment named next closes over whatever has just been listed.

blocks.note: Royal Ascot is the June race meeting whose Royal Enclosure still requires a hat, so that is what you are dressed in; the three letters split after the first
the Roman numeral for one
a tout is the man at the racecourse selling tips

annotation.surface: Telling off a racing tipster who has turned up in his Ascot finery.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole surface is a day at the races, and the one thing the clue asks you to put on is what everybody there is wearing. 'One' is the numeral, not the pronoun standing in for a person.
annotation.definitionFit: To hit out at somebody is to attack them in words, the phrase headlines use for a minister hitting out at critics, which is criticising them.

entries.clue: Operation where end of scalpel slices through Afro/Cornish meat dish? (11)

indicatorNotes.end of: The end of a word is its final letter, which is all this one hands over.
indicatorNotes.slices through: A slice through something cuts into the middle of it, so the letter lands inside the piece it cuts.

blocks.note: the African side of the slash: the rhinoceros is the beast of the African plains
the Cornish pasty is the crimped pastry case of beef, potato and swede that tin miners carried underground; it opens after its first letter
the last letter of scalpeL

annotation.surface: The tip of a scalpel cutting through some improbable Afro-Cornish supper.
annotation.walkthrough: The slash is the instruction: one word for the African side, another for the Cornish, and only the second of them is a meat dish. The nose is what this surgery reshapes, which is the joke in picking that particular African animal.
annotation.definitionFit: Rhinoplasty is the surgical reshaping of the nose, a nose job, so 'operation' names it by the general kind of procedure it is.

entries.clue: ‘arbour used regularly as street (6)

indicatorNotes.regularly: Letters taken regularly come at even intervals, every other one, rather than all of them.

blocks.note: a harbour is a haven, and the apostrophe marking a dropped aitch takes the H off the front of HAVEN
every other letter of Used gives U and E

annotation.surface: A leafy arbour so regularly walked through that it might as well be a road.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is not decoration: it marks an aitch dropped in speech, so the word wanted is what a harbour offers a ship, minus its first letter. 'Regularly' then does its ordinary job on the four letters beside it.
annotation.definitionFit: An avenue is a broad road, usually lined with trees, and street names on both sides of the Atlantic use the two words interchangeably.

entries.clue: Towards the back, seat adjusted before service (6)

indicatorNotes.adjusted: To adjust a thing is to shift it from where it sat, and letters shifted about come out in a new order.

blocks.note: the four letters of 'seat' in another order
RN is the Royal Navy, one of the armed services

annotation.surface: Shifting a seat about before the service starts.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Service' is the armed-forces sense, and the navy's two letters are the ones a nautical answer wants. The surface is a congregation settling into a pew instead.
annotation.definitionFit: Astern means at or towards the rear of a ship, the direction you look to see the wake, so it is 'towards the back' in nautical dress.

entries.clue: Gorilla somewhere in Cornwall, where hilly? (4)

blocks.note: Goonhilly Downs, the heath on the Lizard peninsula where the satellite dishes stand
the back half of that name is the word 'hilly' itself, and it comes away

annotation.surface: A thug lurking somewhere in the hilly part of Cornwall.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Where hilly?' is a question about the name rather than the landscape — the Downs are flat heath — and what remains when those five letters come off the end is the entry. A gorilla in slang is a heavy, a man kept for his muscle.
annotation.definitionFit: A goon is a hired thug or bruiser, and 'gorilla' is the same slang from the other direction, the big man brought along to frighten people.

entries.clue: What lover of Cornwall might do, scoffing English biscuits (10)

indicatorNotes.scoffing: To scoff is to eat a thing up, so the letters round it swallow the one named next.

blocks.clueFragment: What lover of Cornwall might do
blocks.note: to dig something, in the old slang, is to be fond of it, and St Ives is the artists' town on the Cornish coast
e is the standard abbreviation for English

annotation.surface: An enthusiast for Cornwall wolfing down a packet of English biscuits.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dig' for 'like' is 1960s slang and the clue leans on it without warning, which is what makes those first six words so hard to read as letters. The definition is the final word alone.
annotation.definitionFit: Digestives are the plain wheatmeal biscuits in every British cupboard, named for the bicarbonate once thought to settle the stomach, so 'biscuits' names them by type.

entries.clue: Country where Eden Project failed, say: ultimately foolhardy exercise (5)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: What comes ultimately comes last of all, so only the final letter of the word beside it is wanted.

blocks.note: e.g. is short for 'for example', which is what 'say' does in a sentence
the last letter of foolhardY
PT is physical training, the British school timetable's name for gym

annotation.surface: A country where an Eden project came to nothing, plus a rash bit of exercise.
annotation.walkthrough: The Eden of the definition is Anthony Eden, the prime minister whose Suez adventure collapsed in 1956, while the surface wants you picturing the biomes in a Cornish clay pit. 'Say' looks like a marker for an example and is two letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Egypt is where Eden's Suez project failed in 1956, the invasion that ended his premiership, so the definition names the country by that disaster.

entries.clue: Reminder, a few seconds for myself? (4)

blocks.note: me is the word you use of yourself
a mo is a moment — hang on a mo

annotation.surface: Sparing myself a couple of seconds.
annotation.walkthrough: The two halves arrive in the answer the other way round from the clue, which the word 'for' quietly allows. The question mark is there because a note to oneself is the very thing being described.
annotation.definitionFit: A memo is the short note written so something is not forgotten, which is what a reminder does.

entries.clue: Less emphatically, train finally coming in late? (3,6)

indicatorNotes.finally: What comes finally is the last of a word, so that single letter is all this takes.
indicatorNotes.coming in: Something coming in arrives inside, so the letter drops into the middle of the phrase named next.

blocks.note: late is not early, spelt out the long way as two words that then open up
the last letter of traiN

annotation.surface: A train coming in late, though nobody is making much of it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Late' is defined the long way round, as its own opposite negated, and the question mark admits the liberty. The 'finally' that sounds like a passenger's exasperation is a letter instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Not nearly' is 'less' said with force: not nearly as good means a long way short of good, which is the definition's 'emphatically'.

entries.clue: Feline with shaved ball? (5)

indicatorNotes.shaved: To shave something is to take off what sits on the outside, so the word loses a letter at each end.

blocks.note: a bouncer is cricket's short-pitched ball, the one that rears at the batter, and shaving it takes the B and the R off its two ends

annotation.surface: A cat, and a ball that has had its nap shaved off.
annotation.walkthrough: The ball is a cricket one: a bouncer is a delivery, not a doorman, and the question mark covers that leap. A shave comes off the outside, which is why both ends go rather than just the front.
annotation.definitionFit: The ounce is the snow leopard of the high Himalaya, a genuine cat and one of the crossword's regular ones.

entries.clue: Group experiencing the blues record (3,4)

blocks.note: a set is a group of things that belong together
somebody down is low in spirits

annotation.surface: A band with the blues making a record.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Record' is the verb — to set something down is to write it out — while the surface dresses it as the noun a group would release. 'The blues' is doing the same double duty, a music and a mood.
annotation.definitionFit: To set down is to commit something to paper, as in setting down your thoughts in a letter, which is what 'record' asks for as a verb.

entries.clue: Article with check so enclosed? (7)

blocks.note: the definite article
to rein a horse is to check it, pulling it up short

annotation.surface: A written article sent off with a payment enclosed.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is the last two words and it points back at the clue itself: the article and the check really are enclosed in what you write. 'Check' is the rider's verb, not the American spelling of the cheque the surface suggests.
annotation.definitionFit: Therein means inside that thing — therein lies the problem — so 'so enclosed' describes anything held within, which is where the clue's own two pieces sit.
